mcqs.question: A $100 transfer debits account A and credits account B. Which ACID property specifically guarantees that a crash can never leave the debit applied without the credit?
options: Consistency, because the total balance invariant would be violated
Atomicity, because the two writes are treated as one indivisible unit
Isolation, because the two writes must not overlap with other transactions
Durability, because the writes must survive a crash
mcqs.explanation: Atomicity is specifically the all-or-nothing guarantee across the statements in a transaction. Consistency describes the resulting state being valid, isolation is about concurrent transactions not seeing each other's half-done work, and durability is about surviving a crash after commit, not during a crash mid-transaction.

mcqs.question: Why can rolling back a transaction that updated 10 million rows in InnoDB take longer than the original write?
options: ROLLBACK re-reads every row from disk to verify it before undoing it
InnoDB must acquire fresh locks on all 10 million rows before it can roll back
Rollback has to walk and apply the undo log entries for every one of those writes
InnoDB always rewrites the entire table file on any rollback
mcqs.explanation: InnoDB implements atomicity via an undo log, and rolling back means applying undo records to restore old values — the cost scales with how much was written. It doesn't need to re-verify rows from disk, doesn't re-acquire fresh locks as the special cost driver, and doesn't rewrite the whole table file.

mcqs.question: Your database process crashes immediately after a client receives a successful COMMIT response. Under what condition is that committed write guaranteed to survive?
options: As long as the write was applied to the in-memory buffer pool before the crash
As long as the commit record was fsync'd to durable storage before COMMIT returned
As long as the table has a primary key defined
As long as the transaction was wrapped in an explicit BEGIN/COMMIT block rather than autocommit
mcqs.explanation: Durability depends on the commit record reaching durable storage via fsync before the client is told the commit succeeded — an in-memory buffer or OS page cache write alone can be lost on power loss. A primary key and explicit transaction boundaries are unrelated to whether the commit itself was fsync'd.

mcqs.question: A transaction stays open for 10 minutes while your app waits on a slow third-party API call. In Postgres, what's the most likely production consequence?
options: Nothing, since Postgres transactions have no cost while idle
The transaction automatically commits after a timeout, silently applying partial work
It pins the oldest snapshot VACUUM must respect, blocking cleanup and causing table bloat, and can hold locks other writers need
Postgres automatically converts it to a read-only transaction to protect other writers
mcqs.explanation: A long-open transaction in an MVCC engine prevents VACUUM from reclaiming dead row versions newer than its snapshot, causing bloat, and if it has taken any row locks it blocks other writers too. Postgres does not auto-commit on a timeout by default, and idle transactions are not free.

mcqs.question: You need to update an order in the order-service database and charge a card via the payment-service database in the same logical operation. Why isn't this simply "an ACID transaction"?
options: ACID as classically defined applies to one database node's own data, so crossing databases needs extra machinery like two-phase commit or a saga
ACID only applies to read operations, never to writes that touch money
Two-phase commit is built into every database automatically, so this already works without any extra code
Sagas make the operation just as atomic as a single-node transaction, with no trade-offs
mcqs.explanation: Classic ACID guarantees are scoped to a single database instance. Spanning two databases requires deliberately added coordination — two-phase commit (which blocks on the slowest participant) or a saga (which trades true atomicity for eventual consistency plus compensating actions). Neither comes for free, and ACID isn't limited to reads.
